lessons.title: Inferring dependencies with Armstrong rules
lessons.summary: Which dependencies follow from others: Armstrong's rules, the rules derived from them, and the left-side trap.
lessons.body:
## Armstrong's axioms

Given some FDs, which others must also hold? William Armstrong gave three inference rules in 1974. For attribute sets X, Y and Z:

1. **Reflexivity**: a set determines any subset of itself.
2. **Augmentation**: adding the same attributes to both sides keeps an FD true.
3. **Transitivity**: if X determines Y and Y determines Z, then X determines Z.

```formula reference
Y ⊆ X gives X → Y
X → Y gives XZ → YZ
X → Y and Y → Z gives X → Z
where
X, Y, Z: sets of attributes of one relation
⊆: is a subset of: every attribute of Y is in X
→: functionally determines
XZ, YZ: sets written side by side are combined: XZ means X ∪ Z, the attributes of X together with those of Z
∪: union: everything in either set
In words: a set determines its own parts (reflexivity); adding the same attributes to both sides keeps a rule true (augmentation); and rules chain (transitivity).
```

The rules have **soundness** (every conclusion follows from the given FDs) and **completeness** (every FD that follows from those premises can be derived). Three useful rules follow from them:

- The **FD union rule**: if X determines Y and X determines Z, X determines both together.
- The **decomposition rule**: if X determines Y and Z together, it determines each of them.
- **Pseudotransitivity**: if X determines Y, and W together with Y determines Z, then W together with X determines Z. Chains still work when the second rule needs extra attributes.

```formula reference
X → Y and X → Z gives X → YZ
X → YZ gives X → Y and X → Z
X → Y and WY → Z gives WX → Z
where
W, X, Y, Z: sets of attributes of one relation
→: functionally determines
YZ, WY, WX: combined sets, for example YZ = Y ∪ Z
∪: union: everything in either set
In words: the FD union rule combines right sides that share a left side; decomposition splits a right side apart; pseudotransitivity chains two FDs even when the second one needs extra attributes on its left.
```

> [!warning] The left side does not decompose
> A right side can be split, but a left side cannot. Grade depends on student *and* course together, not on either alone. One counterexample settles it: student 1 with grade A in DB and grade B in AI satisfies "student and course fix the grade" but breaks "student alone fixes the grade".

The **FD closure** of a set of dependencies contains every dependency that set implies, trivial ones included. It can be exponentially large, so in practice you never list it. To answer "does this rule follow?", you compute the attribute closure of one left side instead: the next unit.

## Key takeaways

- Reflexivity, augmentation and transitivity derive exactly the implied FDs.
- Right sides split; left sides generally do not. Counterexamples refute invalid inference.

## Further reading

- [Silberschatz, Korth and Sudarshan: relational database design](https://www.db-book.com/slides-dir/PDF-dir/ch7.pdf)
- [Armstrong's axioms (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armstrong%27s_axioms)

questions.prompt: Attributes A, B, C and D satisfy exactly two stated dependencies: A fixes B, and B together with C fixes D. Which dependencies are implied by these two? Select all that apply.

options.text: A and C together determine D
options.explanation: Correct. A gives B; together with the initial C, this gives D. This is pseudotransitivity.

options.text: A alone determines D
options.explanation: A reaches only itself and B. The dependency deriving D also needs C, which cannot be obtained.

options.text: A and C together determine both B and D
options.explanation: Correct. Starting from A and C reaches all four attributes, including both requested right-side attributes.

options.text: B alone determines D
options.explanation: B alone reaches only B; deriving D also requires C.

options.text: A and B together determine B
options.explanation: Correct. A set always determines an attribute already contained in itself; this is reflexivity.

questions.workedExample:
For each option, start from its left side and apply the given rules until nothing new appears, then check whether every requested attribute was reached:

1. From A and C: A gives B, then B with C gives D. Everything is reached, so the first and third options follow (the first is pseudotransitivity).
2. From A alone: A gives B, but the rule for D also needs C, which nothing derives. D is not reached.
3. From B alone: nothing fires, because the rule for D needs C too.
4. A and B together determine B trivially: a set always determines its own members (reflexivity).

So the implied dependencies are the first, third and fifth options.

lessons.title: Computing attribute closure
lessons.summary: Attribute closure: start from what you know, keep applying dependencies until nothing new appears.
lessons.body:
## The attribute-closure algorithm

An **attribute closure** collects every attribute determined by a chosen starting set under the given FD basis. Compute it with a fixpoint loop:

1. Start with the requested attribute set as the result.
2. Find any given FD whose whole left side is already in the result. Add its right side to the result.
3. Repeat until nothing changes.

Because the set only ever grows, and it can never grow beyond the relation's attributes, the loop must stop. The final set is the attribute closure of the starting set: exactly the attributes it determines.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: cooking from a well-stocked cupboard
> You start with some ingredients and a recipe book. Any recipe whose ingredients you all have can be made, and what you make (pastry, a sauce) unlocks further recipes. Keep going until no recipe gives you anything new: that is everything you can produce.
>
> **How it maps:** Your starting ingredients are the starting attribute set, each recipe is a dependency (all of its left side must be present), and what you can eventually produce is the attribute closure. A recipe needing two ingredients waits until you have both, just as a two-attribute left side does.
>
> **Where it stops:** Cooking uses up ingredients and a recipe can fail. Deriving an attribute consumes nothing and always succeeds, and the order in which you apply rules cannot change the final set.

The same algorithm in Python, with a set of letters standing for attributes:

```python
def closure(attrs, fds):
    # Start with the known attributes.
    result = set(attrs)
    changed = True
    while changed:
        changed = False
        # Fire every applicable dependency.
        for lhs, rhs in fds:
            if lhs <= result \
               and not rhs <= result:
                # Add new attributes.
                result |= rhs
                changed = True
    return result

F = [({'A'}, {'B'}),
     ({'B'}, {'C'}),
     ({'C', 'D'}, {'E'})]
print(sorted(closure({'A'}, F)))
# ['A', 'B', 'C']
print(sorted(closure({'A', 'D'}, F)))
# ['A', 'B', 'C', 'D', 'E']
```

Trace the attribute closure of A and D together for a relation with attributes A to E and the three dependencies in the code (A fixes B, B fixes C, C with D fixes E). The first dependency adds B to the known A and D. The second then adds C; with C and D available, the third adds E. A sequential Python pass can fire a later rule using an attribute added earlier in that same pass. Applying the rules in simultaneous rounds instead takes a different route but reaches the same final set.

Textbooks, and the later units here, write the attribute closure of a set with a superscript plus:

```formula reference
{A, D}⁺ = {A, B, C, D, E}
where
{A, D}⁺: the attribute closure of the set {A, D}: every attribute that A and D together determine under the given dependencies. A superscript plus after an attribute set always means its attribute closure
A, B, C, D, E: the attributes of the relation in the trace
{ }: a set of attributes
In words: the attribute closure of A and D together is the whole heading, so A and D together form a superkey of this relation.
```

Each pass of the loop either adds at least one attribute or changes nothing and stops. So the number of passes is at most one per attribute, plus a final pass that finds nothing new, and each pass checks every dependency once. The algorithm runs in polynomial time and is fast in practice, which is why it, rather than listing every implied dependency, is the everyday tool.

## Key takeaways

- Start from known attributes and apply every available FD until a full pass adds nothing.
- The order of firing does not matter: every schedule reaches the same final set.

## Further reading

- [Silberschatz, Korth and Sudarshan: relational database design](https://www.db-book.com/slides-dir/PDF-dir/ch7.pdf)
- [Functional dependency, including attribute closure (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Functional_dependency)

questions.prompt:
A reporting table `order_item(order_id, customer_id, customer_email, product_id, qty)` follows these business rules: an order belongs to one customer; a customer has one email address; and the quantity belongs to an order and product together.

A developer wants to know everything that `order_id` alone pins down, to decide whether it could identify a row. What is the attribute closure of `order_id`?

options.text: `order_id` and `customer_id`
options.explanation: This applies the first rule but stops too soon. Once `customer_id` is known, the email rule fires too.

options.text: `order_id`, `customer_id` and `customer_email`
options.explanation: Correct. The order fixes the customer, the customer fixes the email, and nothing more fires: the quantity rule also needs `product_id`, which nothing derives.

options.text: All five attributes, so `order_id` is a key
options.explanation: The quantity depends on the order **and** product together, and nothing derives `product_id`. An order has several items, so `order_id` cannot identify one row.

options.text: Only `order_id`
options.explanation: The attribute closure always includes the starting set, but here the order-to-customer rule adds more.

questions.workedExample:
Start from what you know and apply every rule whose whole left side you already have:

1. Known: `order_id`.
2. The order rule fires: add `customer_id`.
3. The customer rule now fires: add `customer_email`.
4. The quantity rule needs `order_id` **and** `product_id`; `product_id` is missing and nothing derives it, so it cannot fire. A further pass adds nothing, so stop.

The attribute closure is `order_id`, `customer_id` and `customer_email`. It is not the whole heading, so `order_id` is not a key of `order_item`; the key must include `product_id`. The result also exposes a design smell: the email depends on a non-key attribute, so it repeats on every item of every order that customer places.

lessons.title: Applying attribute closure
lessons.summary: Using attribute closure to test implications and superkeys and to compare dependency sets.
lessons.body:
## Three jobs for attribute closure

1. **Does a given FD follow from the rules?** Compute the attribute closure of its left side and check that its right side is inside it.
2. **Is a set of attributes a superkey?** Yes exactly when its attribute closure is the whole heading.
3. **Do two rule sets say the same thing?** Yes if every FD in each set follows from the other set.

```formula reference
F ⊨ X → Y iff Y ⊆ X⁺
X⁺ = R
F ≡ G iff F⁺ = G⁺
where
F, G: two sets of FDs over the same relation
X, Y: sets of attributes
→: functionally determines
⊨: logically implies: every relation state satisfying F also satisfies the FD on the right
⊆: is a subset of
X⁺: the attribute closure of X under F
R: the set of all attributes of the relation; X⁺ = R means X is a superkey
≡: equivalent: F and G imply exactly the same FDs
F⁺, G⁺: the FD closures of F and G: every FD each one implies
In words: a rule follows when everything on its right side is in the attribute closure of its left side; a set is a superkey when its attribute closure is the whole heading; and two rule sets are equivalent when they imply exactly the same rules.
```

## Using attribute closure on a real design

Take a reporting table `order_item(order_id, customer_id, customer_email, product_id, qty)` with three business rules: an order belongs to one customer, a customer has one email, and the quantity belongs to an order and product together.

- **Is `order_id` a key?** Its attribute closure is the order id, customer id and email. That is not the whole heading, so no: one order has several items.
- **Is the order and product pair a key?** Its attribute closure picks up the customer and email through the order, and the quantity through the pair: the whole heading. It is a superkey, and since neither half alone reaches everything, it is a candidate key.
- **Does "order determines email" follow?** The attribute closure of the order id contains the email, so yes. It is never stated directly, yet it holds: a fact worth knowing, because it means the email is repeated on every item of every order.

**Equivalence in practice.** Suppose a refactor deletes the stated rule "order determines email" from the documented rule set, keeping "order determines customer" and "customer determines email". Check each deleted rule against the remaining set: the attribute closure of the order id still reaches the email, so nothing was lost. Test equivalence rule by rule like this, in both directions, rather than ever listing every implied dependency.

## Key takeaways

- The attribute closure of a determinant tests both implication and superkeys.
- Two FD sets are equivalent exactly when each derives all dependencies of the other.

## Further reading

- [Silberschatz, Korth and Sudarshan: relational database design](https://www.db-book.com/slides-dir/PDF-dir/ch7.pdf)
- [Functional dependency (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Functional_dependency)

questions.prompt: A relation with attributes A, B, C, D, E has these functional dependencies: A fixes C; B and C together fix D; D fixes E. Which statement is correct?

options.text: A alone fixes D because A fixes C and B with C fixes D
options.explanation: A derives C, but reaching D also requires B. A alone therefore reaches only A and C; deleting B from the determinant is invalid.

options.text: The pair B and C is a candidate key
options.explanation: The pair B and C reaches B, C, D and E, but never A, so it is not a superkey.

options.text: The pair A and B is the only candidate key
options.explanation: Correct. A and B must both belong to every key because neither can be derived. Together they reach every attribute, so that pair is minimal and every strict superset is not.

options.text: A together with B and D is a candidate key
options.explanation: ABD is a superkey, but not minimal: AB alone already determines everything.

questions.workedExample:
1. Attributes never on a right side: A and B. Nothing can derive them, so they must be in every key.
2. Attribute closure of A and B together: A gives C; then B with C gives D; then D gives E. That is the whole heading, so A with B is a superkey.
3. A alone reaches only A and C, and B alone reaches only B, so neither half is a superkey: the pair is minimal.
4. Every key must contain A and B, and that pair already is a key, so it is the **only** candidate key. Anything larger, such as A, B and D, is a superkey but not minimal.

lessons.title: Finding every candidate key
lessons.summary: Finding every candidate key with two pruning rules, and why stopping at the first key misleads normal-form tests.
lessons.body:
## Finding candidate keys

A **candidate key** is a superkey with no unnecessary attributes: it determines every attribute, and no smaller part of it does.

```formula reference
X⁺ = R
X' ⊂ X gives X'⁺ ≠ R
where
X: the candidate key being tested
X⁺: the attribute closure of X
R: the set of all attributes of the relation
X': any set made by removing at least one attribute from X
⊂: is a proper subset of: contained in X but not equal to it
X'⁺: the attribute closure of X'
≠: is not equal to
In words: a candidate key determines every attribute of the relation, and removing any of its attributes breaks that.
```

Searching every subset is exponential, but two observations prune it hard:

- An attribute that **never appears on any right-hand side** cannot be derived, so it must be in **every** key.
- An attribute that appears **only on right-hand sides**, and in no determinant, is in **no** candidate key: starting with it cannot help derive anything else, so a superkey containing it can derive it from the other attributes. This assumes the stated FDs are the complete constraint basis being analysed.

> [!example] One key
> Use the five-attribute closure example from the preceding unit: A fixes B, B fixes C, and C together with D fixes E. A and D cannot be derived, so every key includes both. Their attribute closure reaches all five attributes; therefore that pair is the only candidate key.

> [!example] Several keys
> In a four-attribute example, A and B together fix C, C fixes D, and D fixes A. B cannot be derived and therefore belongs to every key. B alone reaches only itself; adding any one of A, C or D reaches the whole heading: A with B gives C and then D; B with C gives D and then A; B with D gives A and then C.
>
> The candidate keys are B with A, B with C, and B with D. Every one of the four attributes therefore belongs to some candidate key: each is a **prime attribute**, a fact the 3NF test cares about.

A relation with n attributes can have exponentially many candidate keys. For schemas specified by an FD basis, Lucchesi and Osborn showed that deciding whether a given attribute is prime is NP-complete. Exhaustive enumeration can be practical for a small schema; larger ones may need pruning. This explains why identifying every prime attribute for the 3NF test can be harder than computing one attribute closure.

“Minimal” means minimal under set inclusion, not smallest cardinality among keys. There can be candidate keys of different sizes. When checking minimality of a superkey, it suffices to remove each member in turn: if any proper subset were a superkey, some single-member removal would also be one. Do not stop after finding the first candidate key; prime attributes depend on the union of all of them.

## Key takeaways

- Every key must include attributes that cannot be derived from right sides.
- Check every candidate for inclusion minimality; all candidate keys contribute prime attributes.

## Further reading

- [Silberschatz, Korth and Sudarshan: relational database design](https://www.db-book.com/slides-dir/PDF-dir/ch7.pdf)
- [Candidate key (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Candidate_key)

questions.prompt: A relation with attributes A, B, C, D, E has these functional dependencies: A fixes B; B fixes C; C fixes A; D fixes E. So A, B and C determine each other in a cycle. What are all the candidate keys?

options.text: D alone
options.explanation: D derives E but cannot enter the cycle involving A, B and C, so D alone is not a superkey.

options.text: Only the pair A and D
options.explanation: AD is a key, but A, B and C determine each other in a cycle, so BD and CD work just as well.

options.text: A, B, C and D together
options.explanation: It is a superkey, but far from minimal.

options.text: The pairs A/D, B/D and C/D
options.explanation: Correct. D is never on a right side, so it is in every key; E is only on a right side, so it is in none. Any one of A, B, C determines the other two through the cycle.

questions.workedExample:
1. Never on a right side: D. So D is in every key.
2. Only on a right side: E. So E is in no key.
3. D alone reaches only D and E, so add one of A, B or C. Any one of them brings the other two round the cycle, so D plus any one reaches everything.
4. Each pair is minimal: D alone fails, and A, B or C alone can never reach D.
5. Keys: **A with D, B with D and C with D**.

questions.prompt:
A relation with attributes A, B, C, D has these functional dependencies: A and B together fix C; C fixes D; D fixes A.

Third normal form (3NF), covered in the normal-forms units, allows a dependency whose left side is not a superkey only when the attribute it determines is prime, meaning it belongs to at least one candidate key.

A reviewer finds that A with B is a candidate key, stops there, and reports: "C and D are non-prime, so the dependency of D on C breaks 3NF." What is wrong with the review?

options.text: Nothing; C determines D, C is not a superkey and D is non-prime
options.explanation: D is not non-prime. B with D is also a candidate key, so D is prime and the 3NF condition for the dependency of D on C is satisfied.

options.text: It stopped at one key: B with C and B with D are also candidate keys, so every attribute is prime and this dependency does not break 3NF
options.explanation: Correct. B is in every key, and adding any one of A, C or D to it reaches everything. Prime attributes come from all candidate keys; with every attribute prime, 3NF holds. (Boyce–Codd normal form, a stricter form covered later, still fails because C and D are not superkeys.)

options.text: A with B is not actually a key, because A can be derived from D
options.explanation: A with B does reach every attribute, and neither alone does, so it is a candidate key. Being derivable does not stop an attribute appearing in a key.

options.text: It missed a second violation: D fixes A, and D is not a superkey
options.explanation: D is indeed not a superkey, but A belongs to the candidate key A with B, so A is prime and 3NF permits that dependency. The review's real error is treating C and D as non-prime.

questions.workedExample:
1. B is never on a right side, so it is in every key. B alone reaches only itself.
2. Try B plus one attribute:
   - A with B: gives C, then D. Everything.
   - B with C: C gives D, D gives A. Everything.
   - B with D: D gives A, then A with B gives C. Everything.
3. So there are **three** candidate keys, and together they contain A, B, C and D: every attribute is prime.
4. 3NF allows a non-superkey determinant when the attribute it determines is prime. The dependencies C to D and D to A both point at prime attributes, so 3NF holds.
5. Boyce–Codd normal form (a later unit) drops that exception, so this relation would fail it: C and D are determinants that are not superkeys.

Lesson: normal-form tests depend on **all** candidate keys. Stopping at the first one makes attributes look non-prime when they are not.

lessons.title: Minimal FD covers and FD equivalence
lessons.summary: Removing redundancy from a set of dependencies without changing what it means.
lessons.body:
## Minimal FD cover

Two FD sets can say the same thing with different amounts of redundancy. A **minimal FD cover** here means an equivalent set with singleton right sides and no remaining redundancy. Some texts call a grouped-right-side version a canonical FD cover; these presentation conventions differ, while the implied dependencies agree. Our singleton convention requires:

1. Every right side is a single attribute.
2. No left side has an **extraneous determinant attribute** (one you could drop and still derive the FD).
3. No FD is **redundant** (derivable from the others).

Why bother? Every dependency in a design is a rule someone must enforce or check. A redundant rule is enforced twice, and an oversized left side makes a rule look weaker than it is. A minimal cover states the business rules with nothing redundant, and the 3NF synthesis algorithm starts from one.

### A worked reduction

Start with four stated rules: A fixes B and C together; B fixes C; A fixes B (again); and A with B fixes C.

1. **Split right sides.** "A fixes B and C" becomes "A fixes B" and "A fixes C". The repeated "A fixes B" merges with its copy.
2. **Remove extraneous left-side attributes.** In "A with B fixes C", is B needed? A alone already reaches B, and through B reaches C, so B adds nothing. The rule shrinks to "A fixes C", a duplicate of one we already have.
3. **Remove redundant rules.** "A fixes C" follows from "A fixes B" and "B fixes C" by transitivity, so drop it.

What remains is two rules, A fixes B and B fixes C, with exactly the same meaning as the original four.

```formula reference
F = {A → BC, B → C, A → B, AB → C}
F_min = {A → B, B → C}
where
A, B, C: attributes
F: the original set of FDs
BC, AB: the sets {B, C} and {A, B}
→: functionally determines
F_min: a minimal FD cover of F: an equivalent set with single-attribute right sides, no extraneous left-side attributes and no redundant rules
{ }: a set
In words: the four original rules and the two remaining ones imply exactly the same dependencies, so the shorter set says everything the longer one did.
```

Always re-check equivalence after a reduction: each removed rule must still follow from what remains. Minimal FD covers are not always unique; different removal orders can give different, equally valid answers.

## Key takeaways

- A singleton-right-side minimal FD cover removes extraneous left attributes and redundant dependencies.
- Equivalent covers have the same implications and need not be unique.

## Further reading

- [Silberschatz, Korth and Sudarshan: relational database design](https://www.db-book.com/slides-dir/PDF-dir/ch7.pdf)
- [Canonical cover (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canonical_cover)

questions.prompt: A set of functional dependencies says: A fixes B and C together; B fixes C; A and B together fix D. What is a minimal FD cover of this set: an equivalent set with single-attribute right sides, no unneeded left-side attributes and no redundant dependencies?

options.text: A fixes B; B fixes C; A fixes D
options.explanation: Correct. Split the right side, drop B from the determinant fixing D because A already derives B, then remove the direct A-to-C dependency implied by the chain through B.

options.text: A fixes B; A fixes C; B fixes C; A with B fixes D
options.explanation: Splitting right sides is only the first stage. B is still unnecessary in the determinant fixing D, and the direct A-to-C dependency is redundant.

options.text: A fixes B, C and D together (one rule)
options.explanation: This does not meet the singleton-right-side convention, and loses the independent rule that B fixes C.

options.text: A fixes B; B fixes C; B fixes D
options.explanation: Starting from B reaches only B and C. Making B fix D is a stronger, unsupported constraint.

questions.workedExample:
1. **Split right sides:** A fixes B, A fixes C, B fixes C, and A with B fixes D.
2. **Extraneous left attributes:** in "A with B fixes D", A alone already reaches B (and then C and D), so B is unnecessary. The rule becomes "A fixes D".
3. **Redundant rules:** "A fixes C" follows from A fixing B and B fixing C, so drop it.
4. **Check nothing else can go:** without "A fixes B", A would reach only D; without "B fixes C", nothing reaches C from B; without "A fixes D", nothing reaches D. All three are needed.

Result: A fixes B, B fixes C, A fixes D. From A it still reaches everything, exactly as the original set did.

questions.prompt: A set F of functional dependencies says: A fixes B; B fixes C; A fixes C. Two FD sets are equivalent when each implies every dependency of the other. Which of these FD sets are **equivalent** to F? Select all that apply.

options.text: A fixes B; B fixes C
options.explanation: Correct. The two-step chain through B supplies the omitted direct rule fixing C from A, and every rule in this set is in the original.

options.text: A fixes B; A fixes C
options.explanation: Here B determines only itself, so the original rule fixing C from B is lost.

options.text: A fixes B and C together; B fixes C
options.explanation: Correct. Splitting the combined right side recovers both rules from A, while the rule fixing C from B is retained.

options.text: A fixes C; C fixes B
options.explanation: This wrongly adds a rule fixing B from C, and cannot recover the original rule fixing C from B.

questions.workedExample:
Two rule sets are equivalent when each implies every rule of the other. The original set is: A fixes B, B fixes C, A fixes C. The rule that decides this question is "B fixes C", because it is the only one starting from B.

1. **First option:** it keeps "B fixes C", and the chain A to B to C restores "A fixes C". Nothing new is added. Equivalent.
2. **Second option:** starting from B reaches only B, so "B fixes C" is lost. Not equivalent.
3. **Third option:** "A fixes B and C together" splits into the two rules from A, and "B fixes C" is kept. Equivalent.
4. **Fourth option:** starting from B reaches only B, so "B fixes C" is lost; and it claims "C fixes B", which the original never implies (starting from C there reaches only C). Not equivalent.

lessons.title: Dependencies in PostgreSQL queries
lessons.summary: Where dependencies appear in practice: PostgreSQL GROUP BY, data-quality checks and common reasoning mistakes.
lessons.body:
## Where FDs show up in real systems

- **Keys and UNIQUE constraints** directly enforce key-based dependencies. SQL has no general FUNCTIONAL DEPENDENCY declaration for an arbitrary dependency between two sets of columns; some special dependencies can be enforced with CHECK or exclusion constraints, and others need triggers or schema decomposition. Normalisation avoids storing the same dependent fact in many rows.
- **Postgres uses FDs in GROUP BY.** If you group by a table's primary key, PostgreSQL (since version 9.1) lets you select that table's other columns without listing them, because it knows the key determines them. It recognises only primary keys for this: grouping by a `UNIQUE NOT NULL` column, or by a column that a join makes equal to the key, is still rejected.

```sql
SELECT c.id, c.name, COUNT(*)
FROM customer c
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
-- Grouping the PK fixes the name.
GROUP BY c.id;
```

- **Optimisers use keys and FDs.** PostgreSQL's planner drops `GROUP BY` columns that are already determined by the table's primary key (since 9.6) or, from version 18, by a unique index on NOT NULL columns, and it uses unique keys to prove that a join cannot multiply rows.
- **Data-quality checks** test candidate FDs against stored rows. With both `cid` and `ctitle` constrained `NOT NULL`, grouping by course code and requiring more than one distinct title finds violations. `COUNT(DISTINCT ...)` ignores NULLs; do not silently treat its result as an FD proof when missing titles are allowed.

```sql
-- Find codes with conflicting titles.
SELECT cid FROM sheet
GROUP BY cid
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT ctitle) > 1;
```

## Common mistakes

- **Reading FDs off sample data.** A coincidence in 50 rows is not a rule.
- **Splitting the left side.** Two attributes determining a third together does not imply that either one does alone.
- **Forgetting transitivity.** When asked for keys, compute the attribute closure; do not eyeball it. Chains through two FDs are easy to miss.
- **Stopping at one key.** A relation can have several candidate keys, and normal-form tests depend on all of them.

A typical missed chain: D fixes A, and A together with B fixes C, so B together with D also fixes C, even though no stated rule has B and D on its left. Computing the attribute closure of B and D finds it; eyeballing the list of rules does not.

## Key takeaways

- PostgreSQL recognises its base-table primary-key grouping rule, not every logically inferable FD.
- Distinct-value checks can refute an FD when missing values are handled explicitly.

## Further reading

- [Silberschatz, Korth and Sudarshan: relational database design](https://www.db-book.com/slides-dir/PDF-dir/ch7.pdf)
- [PostgreSQL 18: SELECT, GROUP BY and functional dependency](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/sql-select.html)

questions.prompt:
In Postgres, `customer(id PRIMARY KEY, name)` and `orders(id, customer_id)`. Which query fails with "column must appear in the GROUP BY clause"?

```sql
-- Q1
SELECT c.id, c.name, COUNT(*)
FROM customer c JOIN orders o
  ON o.customer_id = c.id
GROUP BY c.id;

-- Q2
SELECT o.customer_id, c.name,
       COUNT(*)
FROM customer c JOIN orders o
  ON o.customer_id = c.id
GROUP BY o.customer_id;
```

options.text: Q1 only
options.explanation: Q1 groups by customer's primary key, so Postgres knows c.name is functionally dependent on it and allows it.

options.text: Q2 only
options.explanation: Correct. Postgres only recognises the FD from a table's primary key to the other columns of the same table. o.customer_id equals c.id in every row, but Postgres does not reason through the join condition, so c.name is rejected.

options.text: Both
options.explanation: Q1 is accepted thanks to Postgres's functional-dependency rule for primary keys.

options.text: Neither
options.explanation: Q2 is rejected; Postgres does not infer FDs through join equalities.

questions.workedExample:
1. PostgreSQL's rule (since version 9.1) for these base tables: an ungrouped column is allowed if the grouped columns include the **primary key of that column's table**.
2. Q1: groups by c.id, the PK of customer, so c.name is allowed.
3. Q2: groups by o.customer_id. It is equal to c.id in every joined row, so logically c.name is determined, but Postgres does not use that inference.
4. Fix Q2: keep o.customer_id grouped and add c.id, or add c.name: `GROUP BY o.customer_id, c.id` / `GROUP BY o.customer_id, c.name`.

questions.prompt: You suspect `sheet(cid, ctitle, ...)` violates the functional dependency from course code `cid` to course title `ctitle`: each course code should have exactly one title. Assume cid and ctitle are NOT NULL. Which query lists the offending course codes?

options.text: `SELECT cid FROM sheet GROUP BY cid HAVING COUNT(*) > 1`
options.explanation: This finds codes that appear more than once, which is normal: many students take the same course. Repetition is not a violation; disagreement is.

options.text: `SELECT cid FROM sheet GROUP BY cid HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT ctitle) > 1`
options.explanation: Correct. It finds codes associated with more than one distinct title, which is exactly two relational tuples equal on cid but different on ctitle.

options.text: `SELECT DISTINCT cid, ctitle FROM sheet`
options.explanation: This lists the pairs, but you would still have to inspect them by eye to find codes appearing with two titles.

options.text: `SELECT ctitle FROM sheet GROUP BY ctitle HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT cid) > 1`
options.explanation: That tests whether a title fixes the course code, reversing the required direction. Two course codes sharing a title do not violate the original rule.

questions.workedExample:
1. A violation has equal course codes associated with different titles.
2. Group by X (`cid`) and count distinct Y (`ctitle`).
3. Any group with `COUNT(DISTINCT ctitle) > 1` is a violation.
4. Note: `COUNT(DISTINCT ...)` ignores NULLs, so a code with one title and some NULL titles will not show up. Add `OR COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE ctitle IS NULL) > 0` if NULLs matter.

lessons.title: Anomalies and first normal form
lessons.summary: Update, insertion and deletion anomalies from mixing facts in one table, and what first normal form asks for.
lessons.body:
Normalisation is the process of splitting a badly structured relation into smaller ones so that **each fact is stored once**. When a fact is stored in many rows, the copies can disagree unless additional constraints or coordinated writes keep them consistent.

Each normal form forbids one kind of redundancy, defined precisely with the functional dependencies (FDs) from the previous lesson. Kent’s informal summary says that non-key facts should depend on the key, its whole value, and no unrelated determinant. It is a mnemonic; the precise prime-attribute conditions in the following units handle cases the mnemonic misses.

## The problem: anomalies

A shop imports its order spreadsheet as a single table:

```
OrderLine
oid pid odate  cid cname pname  price qty
 10 P1  03-01  C7  Ann   Bolt   0.20  50
 10 P2  03-01  C7  Ann   Nut    0.10  50
 11 P1  03-02  C9  Raj   Bolt   0.20  10
```

The shop's business rules, written as FDs, hold in every legal state, not just in these three rows:

```formula reference
oid → odate, cid
cid → cname
pid → pname, price
{oid, pid} → qty
where
→: functionally determines: rows that agree on the left side must agree on the right side
oid: the order id
odate: the order date
cid: the customer id
cname: the customer's name
pid: the product id
pname: the product's name
price: the product's current price (this shop sets one current price per product)
qty: the quantity of that product on that order
, (on the right of →): both attributes are determined, so oid → odate, cid means oid → {odate, cid}
{ }: a set of attributes; {oid, pid} means "order and product together"
In words: an order fixes its date and customer; a customer fixes their name; a product fixes its name and current price; and the order and product together fix the quantity.
```

The only candidate key is the pair of order id and product id. Three kinds of trouble follow.

1. **Update anomaly.** Ann changes her name. It is stored on every line of every order she has placed, and an update that misses one leaves the data contradicting itself.
2. **Insertion anomaly.** You cannot record a new product until someone orders it, because `oid` is part of the key and cannot be NULL.
3. **Deletion anomaly.** Delete order 11, Raj's only order, and you lose the fact that customer C9 is called Raj.

All three come from FDs whose left side is not a key: the table is storing facts about customers and products inside rows about order lines.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: phone numbers on attendance sheets
> A club secretary keeps no member list. Instead, every weekly attendance sheet records each attendee's name and phone number. When a member changes number, every old sheet still shows the old one. A new member cannot be recorded until they attend a meeting, and shredding the only sheet a member appears on loses their number entirely.
>
> **How it maps:** Each sheet line is an order line, the phone number is a customer fact stored on it, and the three troubles are the update, insertion and deletion anomalies. A separate member list, referenced by membership number, is the normalised Customer table.
>
> **Where it stops:** Old attendance sheets might rightly keep the number that was valid on the day, which is a historical fact, not a copy. In a database you must decide which you mean: a current fact belongs in one place, a fact as it was at the time belongs with the event.

## First normal form (1NF)

A relation is in 1NF when every attribute value is an **atomic relational value**: a single value from its domain, with no repeating groups.

```
Not 1NF
oid  products
 10  "P1:50, P2:50"
```

Ordinary column constraints and joins do not directly represent the individual items; string-splitting expressions or custom constraints are more complex than storing a row per item. The fix is one row per product per order, as in OrderLine above.

> [!note] What counts as atomic?
> Atomicity is relative to the chosen domains and relational presentation. Decomposability by a function does not alone violate 1NF: dates and text have inspectable parts. Under the classical flat-relation convention used here, a repeating collection of phone numbers or order lines is represented by separate relational tuples. SQL arrays and JSON are valid SQL values with useful operators, but calling them automatically in or out of 1NF merely because an application searches inside them is too broad. For this design, separate rows let each phone or line have ordinary keys, foreign keys and indexes.

## Key takeaways

- Mixing order, customer and product facts creates update, insertion and deletion anomalies.
- Use separate relational tuples for repeating phone or item facts under the flat relational convention.

## Further reading

- [Silberschatz, Korth and Sudarshan: relational database design](https://www.db-book.com/slides-dir/PDF-dir/ch7.pdf)
- [Fagin: multivalued dependencies and fourth normal form](https://research.ibm.com/publications/multivalued-dependencies-and-a-new-normal-form-for-relational-databases)

questions.prompt: A single flat `OrderLine` table repeats customer id `cid` and name `cname` on each order/product line. Its key is the order id `oid` together with product id `pid`. Customer C9 (Raj) appears only on order 11. You delete order 11, which is Raj's only order. Afterwards nobody can find out what customer C9 is called. Which anomaly is this?

options.text: Update anomaly
options.explanation: An update anomaly is about changing one fact that is stored in many rows and missing a copy. Nothing was updated here.

options.text: Insertion anomaly
options.explanation: An insertion anomaly is being unable to record a fact (for example a new customer) without an unrelated one (an order).

options.text: Deletion anomaly
options.explanation: Correct. Deleting one fact (the order) unintentionally deleted another (the customer's name), because both lived in the same rows.

options.text: Referential integrity violation
options.explanation: No foreign key is broken; there is no separate Customer table to reference yet. That is exactly the design problem.

questions.workedExample:
1. `cname` depends on non-key cid; the key {oid, pid} also determines it transitively.
2. So customer facts exist only as a side effect of order lines.
3. Remove Raj's last line and the fact "C9 is Raj" goes with it: a **deletion anomaly**.
4. After normalising, `Customer(cid, cname)` keeps Raj even with no orders.

questions.prompt: A `contact` table has a column `phones` holding values like `'020 7946 0000; 07700 900123'`. Support staff need to search for a customer by any one phone number. Under the classical flat-relation convention, where each phone is a separate domain value rather than a collection, which normal form is being violated, and what is the usual fix?

options.text: 2NF; move phones into a table keyed by part of the primary key
options.explanation: 2NF is about partial dependencies on a composite key. The problem here is a non-atomic relational value inside one column.

options.text: 1NF; store one row per phone number in a `contact_phone(contact_id, phone)` table
options.explanation: Correct. The column holds a repeating group. Because staff must search on a single number, each number should be its own value, which also lets you index and constrain it.

options.text: 3NF; phones depend transitively on the contact's id
options.explanation: There is no transitive dependency here. The issue is that one attribute value holds several values.

options.text: None; a semicolon-separated string is atomic because it is one text value
options.explanation: A SQL text value can contain delimiters, and searching inside text does not by itself define 1NF. Under the classical flat representation stipulated here, however, the phone-number collection is a repeating group; separate rows provide ordinary indexing and per-number constraints.

questions.workedExample:
1. 1NF requires atomic relational values, with no repeating groups.
2. The modelling requirement is one searchable, constrainable phone-number fact per row. Querying a component of a value does not universally determine atomicity: dates and text have components too. Separate phone rows implement the flat convention and the stated requirement.
3. Fix:

```sql
CREATE TABLE contact_phone (
  contact_id INT REFERENCES contact,
  phone      TEXT,
  PRIMARY KEY (contact_id, phone));
```

4. For efficient searches by phone alone, add an index on phone. The composite primary-key index starts with contact_id; a planner may scan it or use skip scan, but a direct phone index is the straightforward access path.

lessons.title: Second normal form and partial dependence
lessons.summary: Second normal form: diagnosing attributes that depend on only part of a composite key.
lessons.body:
This unit continues the shop design: an order line stores order id `oid`, product id `pid`, date `odate`, customer id `cid`, customer name `cname`, product name `pname`, current product price `price`, and quantity `qty`. An order has one customer and date; a product has one current name and price. One line per order and product is the business rule.

## Second normal form (2NF)

A relation is in 2NF when it is in 1NF and **no non-prime attribute depends on part of a candidate key**. (A **prime** attribute is one that belongs to some candidate key.)

```formula reference
X ↛ A
  for every X ⊂ K and every A ∉ P
where
K: any candidate key of the relation
X: a set of attributes that is part of K but not all of it
⊂: is a proper subset of: inside K, and smaller than K
A: a single attribute
P: the set of prime attributes: those that belong to at least one candidate key
∉: is not a member of; A ∉ P means A is non-prime
↛: does not functionally determine
In words: no non-prime attribute may be determined by only part of a candidate key.
```

In practice, a **partial dependency** needs a composite key: a single-attribute key has no smaller non-empty part. (The one technical exception is a non-prime column forced to hold a single constant value, which the empty set of attributes "determines"; the schemas here have none.) So the 2NF question to ask of a table is: *does any non-key fact depend on only some of the key's columns?*

OrderLine's key is the order/product pair, and each half determines attributes on its own:

```formula reference
oid → odate, cid, cname
pid → pname, price
where
→: functionally determines
oid, pid: the order id and product id, each one half of the key {oid, pid}
odate, cid, cname: the order date, customer id and customer name (oid reaches cname through cid)
pname, price: the product's name and current price
, (on the right of →): every listed attribute is determined, so oid → odate, cid, cname means oid determines all three
In words: the order id alone fixes the date and customer (and, through the customer, the customer's name); the product id alone fixes the product's name and price.
```

Both are partial dependencies. Fix them by moving each one into its own relation:

```
Order(oid, odate, cid, cname)
Product(pid, pname, price)
Line(oid, pid, qty)
```

Each order's date and customer are now stored once per order, and each product's name and price once per product. The line keeps only what genuinely needs both halves of the key: the quantity. Order still repeats a customer's name on every order they place; that is a different problem, which third normal form addresses next.

## Key takeaways

- 2NF forbids a non-prime attribute depending on a proper part of any candidate key.
- Separate order and product facts from order-line facts to remove partial dependencies.

## Further reading

- [Silberschatz, Korth and Sudarshan: relational database design](https://www.db-book.com/slides-dir/PDF-dir/ch7.pdf)
- [Fagin: multivalued dependencies and fourth normal form](https://research.ibm.com/publications/multivalued-dependencies-and-a-new-normal-form-for-relational-databases)

questions.prompt: A relation R with attributes A, B, C is in 1NF. Its complete FD basis is a single non-trivial dependency: A alone fixes C. Its only candidate key is the pair A and B. Which is the highest normal form R satisfies?

options.text: 1NF
options.explanation: Correct. C is non-prime and depends on A, which is only part of the key {A, B}. That partial dependency breaks 2NF.

options.text: 2NF
options.explanation: 2NF forbids exactly this: a non-prime attribute (C) depending on part of a candidate key (A).

options.text: 3NF
options.explanation: 3NF implies 2NF, and 2NF already fails.

options.text: BCNF
options.explanation: A alone is not a superkey, so its non-trivial dependency fixing C also violates BCNF.

questions.workedExample:
1. Key: {A, B}. Prime attributes: A, B. Non-prime: C.
2. The stated dependency has determinant A, a proper part of the key, right side C is non-prime. That is a partial dependency.
3. So 2NF fails, and therefore 3NF and BCNF fail too.
4. R is only in **1NF**. Fix: split into (A, C) and (A, B).

lessons.title: Third normal form and indirect facts
lessons.summary: Third normal form: spotting facts that hang off a non-key attribute, and keeping historical prices separate.
lessons.body:
The shop has already separated order lines from product facts. Its remaining Order relation stores order identifier `oid`, order date `odate`, customer identifier `cid` and customer name `cname`. An order fixes its date and customer; a customer fixes one current name. The only candidate key of Order is its order identifier.

## Third normal form (3NF)

A relation is in 3NF when, for every non-trivial FD whose right side is a single attribute A, **either the left side X is a superkey or A is prime**:

```formula reference
for every X → A in F⁺ with A ∉ X:
  X⁺ = R  or  A ∈ P
where
F⁺: every FD that holds on the relation (all FDs implied by the given set F)
X: the left side, a set of attributes
A: the right side, a single attribute
→: functionally determines
∉: is not a member of; A ∉ X makes the FD non-trivial
X⁺: the attribute closure of X; X⁺ = R means X is a superkey
R: the set of all attributes of the relation
∈: is a member of
P: the set of prime attributes (those in some candidate key)
In words: every non-trivial dependency must either come from a superkey or determine an attribute that belongs to some candidate key.
```

The Order relation containing order id, date, customer id and customer name is in 2NF under these rules (its only candidate key is the single order id) but still repeats Ann's name on every order. The cause is a **transitive dependency**: the order fixes the customer, and the customer fixes the name, so the name depends on the key only indirectly, through `cid`. And `cid` determines only itself and the name, not the whole of Order, so it is not a superkey.

With `cid` not a superkey and `cname` not prime, 3NF is violated. Split again:

```
Order(oid, odate, cid)
Customer(cid, cname)
Product(pid, pname, price)
Line(oid, pid, qty)
```

Now every FD's left side is a key of its relation. Ann's name lives in one row, products can exist before anyone orders them, and deleting an order loses nothing else.

> [!tip] A quick 3NF diagnosis
> For each column outside the key, ask which column *actually decides* its value. If the answer is the whole key, fine. If it is another column outside the key (the customer id deciding the customer name), the fact belongs in its own table keyed by that column. The only exception 3NF allows is a determined column that is itself part of some candidate key.

> [!warning] Price is a different fact
> The current price of a product (one per product) can hold in every database state even when prices change over time. It does not imply that the price *paid* on every historical order line equals today's price. In a real shop, the price charged on an order is a separate fact from the current list price, and it belongs to the order and product together: the order id and product id together determine `price_paid`. Store it on `Line`. That is not denormalisation; it is modelling a time-dependent fact correctly. Normalising away the price paid is a classic bug that silently alters old invoices.

## Key takeaways

- 3NF checks every non-trivial singleton-right-side FD for a superkey determinant or prime result attribute.
- Customer name and historical price paid belong to different facts and require different determinants.

## Further reading

- [Silberschatz, Korth and Sudarshan: relational database design](https://www.db-book.com/slides-dir/PDF-dir/ch7.pdf)
- [Fagin: multivalued dependencies and fourth normal form](https://research.ibm.com/publications/multivalued-dependencies-and-a-new-normal-form-for-relational-databases)

lessons.title: BCNF and prime attributes
lessons.summary: Boyce–Codd normal form, and the overlapping-keys case where 3NF passes but redundancy remains.
lessons.body:
## Boyce–Codd normal form (BCNF)

A relation is in BCNF when, for every non-trivial FD that holds in it, **the left side is a superkey**. BCNF drops 3NF's escape clause "or the determined attribute is prime":

```formula reference
for every X → Y in F⁺ with Y ⊄ X:
  X⁺ = R
where
F⁺: every FD that holds on the relation
X, Y: sets of attributes, the left and right sides
→: functionally determines
⊄: is not a subset of; Y ⊄ X makes the FD non-trivial
X⁺: the attribute closure of X
R: the set of all attributes of the relation
In words: every non-trivial dependency must come from a superkey, with no exception for key attributes.
```

A relation can pass 3NF yet fail BCNF only if it has at least two candidate keys that are both composite (made of several attributes) and overlap (share at least one attribute), a condition proved by Vincent and Srinivasan (1993). The condition is necessary, not sufficient: many relations with overlapping composite candidate keys are in BCNF. The classic example: each teacher teaches one course, and each student has one teacher per course. Teaching records student, course and teacher:

```formula reference
{student, course} → teacher
teacher → course
where
student, course, teacher: the three attributes of Teaching
→: functionally determines
{ }: a set of attributes
In words: a student and course fix the teacher, and a teacher fixes the course.
```

Student can never be derived, so it is in every key. Student with course is a key (it gives the teacher); student with teacher is also a key (the teacher gives the course). The two candidate keys overlap on student, so all three attributes are prime. Teacher alone reaches only itself and its course, so it is not a superkey.

- The FD from `teacher` to `course` has a left side that is not a superkey, so **BCNF fails**.
- But `course` is prime (it is in the first candidate key), so **3NF holds**.

The redundancy is real: "Smith teaches DB" is repeated for every student Smith teaches. If Smith switches to teaching AI, every one of those rows must change together, the same update anomaly 3NF was meant to prevent. Fixing it means splitting the table, which the next unit shows has a price.

## Key takeaways

- BCNF requires a superkey determinant for every non-trivial FD.
- Teaching passes 3NF through a prime course attribute while still failing BCNF.

## Further reading

- [Silberschatz, Korth and Sudarshan: relational database design](https://www.db-book.com/slides-dir/PDF-dir/ch7.pdf)
- [Fagin: multivalued dependencies and fourth normal form](https://research.ibm.com/publications/multivalued-dependencies-and-a-new-normal-form-for-relational-databases)

options.explanation: 3NF permits a dependency with a non-superkey determinant when its right-hand attribute is prime. Course belongs to the student/course candidate key.

options.text: It is not even in 2NF

options.text: It is in 3NF but not BCNF
options.explanation: Correct. Both the student/course pair and the student/teacher pair are candidate keys. Teacher alone fixes course but not student: this fails BCNF while passing 3NF because course is prime.

2. **Prime attributes:** student, course and teacher (all three).
3. **BCNF test** on the rule fixing course from teacher: teacher alone reaches only itself and the course, so it is not a superkey. **Fails.**
4. **3NF test:** the left side is not a superkey, but course is prime. **Passes.**
5. So 3NF, not BCNF. The redundancy: "Smith teaches DB" repeats for each of Smith's students.

options.text: R(A, B, C): A fixes B, and B fixes A
options.explanation: The keys are A with C and B with C. A alone fixes B while not being a superkey, so BCNF fails; 3NF holds because B is prime.

options.text: R(A, B, C): A fixes B, and A fixes C
options.explanation: Correct. A is the only candidate key. Every non-trivial implied FD has a determinant containing A, so its determinant is a superkey.

questions.workedExample:
For each schema, find the keys, then check that every rule's left side is a superkey:

1. R(A, B), A fixes B: A is the key. Every rule starts from a superkey. **BCNF.**
2. A and B fix each other; nothing derives C. Keys: A with C, and B with C. "A fixes B" starts from A, which is not a superkey. **Not BCNF** (3NF holds, because B is prime).
3. A fixes both B and C: A is the only key, and every rule starts from A. **BCNF.**
4. Keys: A with B, and B with C. "C fixes A" starts from C, not a superkey. **Not BCNF** (3NF holds, because A is prime).
5. A is the only key. "B fixes C" starts from B, not a superkey, and C is not prime. **Fails both BCNF and 3NF.**

One non-trivial rule whose left side is not a superkey is enough to break BCNF.

lessons.title: Lossless joins and dependency preservation
lessons.summary: Two checks for any table split: can a join rebuild the data exactly, and can each rule still be enforced locally?
lessons.body:
## Decomposing safely

Splitting a relation has two possible costs, and you should check both.

### Lossless join

A decomposition has a **lossless join** if joining the parts always gives back exactly the original relation, in every legal state. If not, the join invents **spurious tuples**. The test for two parts:

```formula essential
(R_1 ∩ R_2) → R_1
  or (R_1 ∩ R_2) → R_2
where
R_1, R_2: the attribute sets of the two parts, together covering the original heading
∩: intersection: the attributes the two parts share
→: functionally determines; here the rule must follow from the given functional dependencies
In words: a two-way split has a lossless join exactly when the shared attributes determine every attribute of at least one part, that is, when they are a superkey of that part.
```

This exact two-part test assumes the only constraints are functional dependencies. The intuition: if the shared attributes identify a single row of one part, each row of the other part can match at most one partner, so the join cannot invent combinations.

Split Teaching badly into `(student, course)` and `(course, teacher)`:

```
student course | course teacher
Ann     DB     | DB     Smith
Bob     DB     | DB     Jones
```

Joining on `course` produces four rows, including `Ann, DB, Jones`, which never happened. Then try the split into `(teacher, course)` and `(student, teacher)` instead.

In the bad split the parts share only `course`, and course determines neither part (a course has several students and, here, two teachers), so the split is lossy. In the good split the parts share `teacher`, and a teacher determines their course, which covers the whole `(teacher, course)` part, so the join is lossless.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: a wedding seating plan
> A planner records which table each guest sits at, and separately which meal each table is served. If every table gets one menu, joining the two lists on table number tells each guest their meal exactly. If table 4 mixes fish and vegetarian, the join assigns every guest at table 4 both meals, and nobody can tell who actually ordered what.
>
> **How it maps:** The two lists are the two parts of a decomposition, table number is the shared attribute, and "one menu per table" is the dependency that makes the shared attribute a key of the table–meal part. Without it, the extra guest–meal pairs are spurious tuples.
>
> **Where it stops:** At a wedding someone would notice the mix-up. A database cannot: a lossy join returns invented rows silently, and the lossless guarantee must come from a rule holding in every legal state, not from how today's tables happen to be seated.

### Dependency preservation

A decomposition **preserves dependencies** if the FDs that hold inside each part, taken together, imply every original FD:

```formula reference
(F_1 ∪ F_2 ∪ ... ∪ F_n)⁺ = F⁺
where
F: the original FDs
F⁺: every FD implied by F
n: the number of parts
F_1, F_2, F_n: the FDs from F⁺ that mention only attributes of part 1, part 2, ..., part n
...: and so on, for every part in between
∪: union: all the FDs together
In words: every original rule can still be enforced one table at a time, without joining the parts back together.
```

Enforcing those local dependencies then suffices without checking a join; an original FD can follow transitively across several local dependencies rather than literally fit in one part. The lossless-join BCNF split of Teaching loses the rule that a student and course together fix the teacher: the projected local FDs do not imply that original rule. For example, local keys still allow Ann to reference Smith and Jones while both teach DB. Merely observing that no part contains all three attributes is not a proof of non-preservation: some dependencies can follow transitively across parts.

## Key takeaways

- Losslessness concerns reconstructing every legal relation without invented relational tuples.
- Dependency preservation concerns whether projected local FDs together imply the original rules.

## Further reading

- [Silberschatz, Korth and Sudarshan: relational database design](https://www.db-book.com/slides-dir/PDF-dir/ch7.pdf)
- [Fagin: multivalued dependencies and fourth normal form](https://research.ibm.com/publications/multivalued-dependencies-and-a-new-normal-form-for-relational-databases)

questions.prompt: A relation with attributes A, B, C has a single functional dependency: A fixes B. Nothing else is known. Which decomposition has a lossless join?

options.text: (A, B) and (A, C)
options.explanation: Correct. The shared A determines both attributes of the first part. Therefore the shared heading is a superkey of that part and the FD-based binary lossless criterion passes.

options.text: (A, C) and (B, C)
options.explanation: They share C, and C determines nothing. Lossy.

options.text: (A, B) and (B, C)
options.explanation: The shared attribute B determines nothing, so it is a key of neither side. Joining on B can pair A and C values that never appeared together.

options.text: Any decomposition has a lossless join as long as every attribute appears in some part
options.explanation: Covering all attributes is necessary but not sufficient; the shared attributes must also determine one side.

questions.workedExample:
The two-part test: a split has a lossless join exactly when the attributes the parts share determine every attribute of at least one part.

1. (A, B) and (A, C) share A. A determines B, so A determines the whole (A, B) part. **Lossless.**
2. (A, C) and (B, C) share C, which determines nothing else. Lossy.
3. (A, B) and (B, C) share B, which determines nothing else. Lossy: joining on B can pair A and C values that never appeared together.

Only (A, B), (A, C) gives a lossless join.

lessons.title: BCNF decomposition and 3NF synthesis
lessons.summary: What BCNF decomposition and 3NF synthesis guarantee, and how to choose when they conflict.
lessons.body:
## The BCNF decomposition algorithm

1. Find a non-trivial dependency, holding within the current table, whose left side is not a superkey of that table.
2. Split the table in two: the left side together with everything it determines (within the table), and the left side together with all the remaining attributes.
3. Repeat on each part until every part is in BCNF.

```formula reference
S_1 = X⁺ ∩ S
S_2 = X ∪ (S − X⁺)
S_1 ∩ S_2 = X
where
S: the relation being split, as a set of attributes
X: the left side of an FD that violates BCNF in S
X⁺: the attribute closure of X under the dependencies projected onto the current schema S; equivalently compute the original attribute closure then intersect with S
∩: intersection: attributes in both
∪: union: attributes in either
−: difference: attributes of S that X does not determine
S_1: X plus everything in S that X determines
S_2: X plus everything else in S
In words: put the offending left side with everything it determines in one part, and the same left side with everything else in the other; the two parts share exactly that left side.
```

Each split shares exactly the offending left side, and that left side determines the whole first part, so by the two-part test every step gives a lossless join.

Take a five-attribute relation where A fixes B, B fixes C, and C together with D fixes E. Its only candidate key is A with D.

1. A fixes B, but A is not a key. Split into the A part (A with what it determines: A, B, C) and the rest (A, D, E).
2. Inside the A, B, C part, B fixes C but B is not a key there (A is). Split into (B, C) and (A, B).
3. The A, D, E part has key A with D, and its only non-trivial rule is that A with D fixes E. It is already in BCNF.

The same split sequence as a schema sketch, with names grouping attributes:

```diagram
Full heading
  |  split on A
  +-- A B C
  |     |  split on B
  |     +-- B C
  |     +-- A B
  +-- A D E
```

All three parts, (B, C), (A, B) and (A, D, E), are in BCNF and the decomposition is lossless-join, but the original rule that C and D together fix E is lost. No part contains C, D and E together, and the rules that hold within the parts (A fixes B, B fixes C, A with D fixes E) cannot derive it: starting from C and D, nothing fires. To enforce that rule now, you would have to check a join.

## The 3NF synthesis algorithm

3NF can always be reached **losslessly while preserving every FD**. The synthesis algorithm builds on Bernstein (1976); the extra key relation in step 3, which guarantees the lossless join, comes from later refinements of his method, notably Biskup, Dayal and Bernstein (1979):

1. Compute a minimal FD cover of the given dependencies.
2. Make one relation for each left side in the cover, containing that left side and everything the cover says it determines.
3. If no relation contains a candidate key of the original relation, add one relation that is just such a key.
4. Drop any relation whose attributes are a subset of another's.

On the same five-attribute example, the three rules are already a minimal cover. One relation per rule gives (A, B), (B, C) and (C, D, E). None of them contains the key A with D, so step 3 adds a fourth relation, (A, D), to tie the parts together.

Result: (A, B), (B, C), (C, D, E) and (A, D). Every original rule lives inside one relation, so each can be enforced by that relation's own key; the key relation makes the decomposition lossless-join; and here each part happens to be in BCNF too. Compare the BCNF result above, which lost the rule that C with D fixes E.

## Choosing between 3NF and BCNF

| | 3NF | BCNF |
|---|---|---|
| Lossless join | always | always |
| FDs preserved | always | not always |
| Redundancy | a little possible | none from FDs |

Check the actual dependencies rather than assuming a frequency of overlapping keys. Many ordinary schemas can reach BCNF while preserving the required FDs; when those goals clash, the choices are:

- Stay in 3NF and accept some redundancy, enforcing the dependencies locally; keys alone may not express every local FD.
- Go to BCNF and enforce the lost FD another way: a trigger or application protocol that checks the joined rule, with locking or a serialisable transaction so two transactions running at the same time cannot both pass the check. PostgreSQL has no general declarative cross-table assertions, and a naive check-then-write can race with another transaction.

## Key takeaways

- BCNF decomposition preserves lossless reconstruction but can lose dependencies.
- 3NF synthesis uses a minimal FD cover and adds a candidate-key relation when needed.

## Further reading

- [Silberschatz, Korth and Sudarshan: relational database design](https://www.db-book.com/slides-dir/PDF-dir/ch7.pdf)
- [Fagin: multivalued dependencies and fourth normal form](https://research.ibm.com/publications/multivalued-dependencies-and-a-new-normal-form-for-relational-databases)

questions.prompt: A relation with attributes A, B, C, D has these functional dependencies: A and B together fix C; C fixes D. Apply the BCNF decomposition algorithm. What is the result, and does it preserve all FDs?

options.text: (A, B, C) and (C, D); preserves all FDs
options.explanation: Correct. C fixes D but is not a superkey of the original. Split C with D into one part, and retain A, B and C in the other. Each original dependency has a local home, and both parts are in BCNF.

options.text: (A, B, C) and (B, C, D); preserves all FDs
options.explanation: This split is lossless, but the B/C/D part still has C fixing D without fixing B, so BCNF is not reached.

options.text: (A, B) and (C, D); preserves all FDs
options.explanation: The parts have no shared attributes, so arbitrary cross-combinations appear; the pair A and B fixing C is also not preserved.

options.text: The A/B/C part and the C/D part; loses the rule that the pair A and B fixes C
options.explanation: The dependency fixing C from the pair A and B fits in the A/B/C part and is preserved.

questions.workedExample:
1. **Key of R.** A and B are never on a right side, and together they reach C and then D: the key is A with B.
2. The rule fixing C from A with B starts from a superkey. Fine.
3. The rule fixing D from C does not: C reaches only C and D. **Violation**, so split on C: put C with what it determines, (C, D), and C with everything else, (A, B, C).
4. (C, D) has key C. (A, B, C) has key A with B, and its only non-trivial rule is that A with B fixes C. Both are in BCNF.
5. **Preservation:** the rule fixing C lives in (A, B, C) and the rule fixing D lives in (C, D). Both are checked locally, so nothing is lost. BCNF decomposition can lose rules, but it does not always.

questions.prompt: Use 3NF synthesis on R(A, B, C, D, E), whose functional dependencies are: A fixes B; C fixes D. No dependency mentions E. What is the result?

options.text: (A, B) and (C, D)
options.explanation: Attribute E is missing altogether, and no part contains a key of R, so the join is lossy.

options.text: (A, B, C, D, E)
options.explanation: A fixes B while not being a superkey, and B is non-prime, so the original relation fails 3NF and must be decomposed.

options.text: (A, B), (C, D) and (E)
options.explanation: (E) holds E but shares no attributes with anything, so joining it is a Cartesian product. Step 3 adds a key relation, not leftover attributes.

options.text: (A, B), (C, D) and (A, C, E)
options.explanation: Correct. The cover gives AB and CD. The candidate key of R is ACE (A, C and E never appear on a right side), and no relation contains it, so add (A, C, E).

questions.workedExample:
1. The two rules (A fixes B, C fixes D) are already a minimal cover.
2. One relation per left side: **(A, B)** and **(C, D)**.
3. Candidate key of R: A, C and E never appear on a right side, so all three are in every key. Together they reach B (from A) and D (from C): everything. So the key is A, C and E.
4. Neither (A, B) nor (C, D) contains that key, so add **(A, C, E)**.
5. Nothing is a subset of another. Result: (A, B), (C, D), (A, C, E). The key relation makes the join lossless, and each rule lives in one relation, so every rule is preserved. Note that E, which no rule mentions, is kept only because the key relation includes it.

questions.prompt: Which statements about decomposition algorithms are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: 3NF synthesis always produces a lossless-join, dependency-preserving decomposition
options.explanation: Correct. That guarantee is the reason to choose 3NF when BCNF would lose an FD.

options.text: BCNF decomposition always produces a lossless-join decomposition
options.explanation: Correct. Each split shares X, and X determines one whole part (X's attribute closure intersected with the relation), so the binary test passes at every step.

options.text: BCNF decomposition always preserves dependencies
options.explanation: False. The Teaching counterexample shows that a BCNF decomposition can lose dependency preservation. In the five-attribute example, the rule fixing E from C together with D is likewise not implied by the projected local FDs.

options.text: Every relation in BCNF is also in 3NF
options.explanation: Correct. BCNF's condition (left side a superkey) is stricter than 3NF's (left side a superkey *or* right side prime).

options.text: Every relation in 3NF is also in BCNF
options.explanation: False. Teaching is in 3NF but not BCNF, because 3NF allows a prime right side with a non-superkey left side.

questions.workedExample:
Summary of the guarantees:

| Algorithm | Lossless join | Preserves FDs |
|---|---|---|
| 3NF synthesis | always | always |
| BCNF decomposition | always | not always |

And the containment between the normal forms runs one way only: every BCNF relation is in 3NF, every 3NF relation is in 2NF, and every 2NF relation is in 1NF, but not the other way round.

lessons.title: Independent facts, 4NF and 5NF
lessons.summary: Independent lists in one table, multivalued dependencies, 4NF and the join dependencies behind 5NF.
lessons.body:
## Beyond BCNF, briefly

BCNF removes redundancy caused by FDs, but not all redundancy. If an employee has a set of skills and, independently, a set of languages, storing `(emp, skill, language)` forces every skill to be paired with every language. That is a **multivalued dependency**: an employee determines a whole *set* of skills, independently of the other attributes.

```formula reference
emp ↠ skill
emp ↠ language
where
emp: the employee
skill: one of the employee's skills
language: one of the languages the employee speaks
↠: multivalued dependency (a double-headed arrow): the left side determines a set of values on the right, and that set does not depend on the remaining attributes
In words: an employee's skills and languages are two independent lists, so every combination ends up stored.
```

**4NF** splits it into `(emp, skill)` and `(emp, language)`. **5NF** handles join dependencies across three or more parts. Both are rare in practice, but the "independent facts in one table" smell is worth recognising.

## The exact condition matters

The dependency says more than “an employee can have several skills”. It requires all combinations of independently recorded skills and languages. Consider one employee with SQL and Python skills and English and French languages:

```
emp skill  language
 7  SQL    English
 7  SQL    French
 7  Python English
 7  Python French
```

There are four combinations. Recording only SQL/English and Python/French would say that the pairs are linked, not independent, and would violate the claimed multivalued dependency. Splitting the independent lists saves repetition while recovering those four rows by a natural join.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: a café's breakfast deal
> A café offers any hot drink with any pastry. Printing the offer as one list of every drink–pastry pair means adding a new pastry adds a line for every drink. Printing two short lists, drinks and pastries, says the same thing, because the choices are independent.
>
> **How it maps:** The café is the employee, drinks and pastries are the skill and language lists, and "any with any" is the multivalued dependency. The long combined list is the table that is not in 4NF; the two short lists are the 4NF decomposition, and pairing them back up is the natural join.
>
> **Where it stops:** If some pastries come only with certain drinks, the choices are not independent and two lists would offer combinations that do not exist. Likewise, splitting a table is only safe when the business guarantees independence for every legal state, not just today's rows.

A multivalued dependency is trivial if its right attributes are already contained in the determinant, or the two sides together cover the whole heading. Fourth normal form requires a superkey determinant for every non-trivial multivalued dependency. Every FD implies an MVD, so this requirement also implies BCNF.

A **join dependency** says that a relation is always exactly the join of specified projections. Fifth normal form, also called project-join normal form, requires every non-trivial join dependency to follow from candidate-key rules. Three-way decompositions can matter even when no useful two-way split exists. Do not infer a join dependency merely because one sample happens to rejoin correctly: it must be a domain rule. Conversely, a supplier/part/project relation with no such rule must keep its three-way facts; splitting can invent combinations.

These are constraint-relative definitions. BCNF does not guarantee freedom from MVD redundancy, and 5NF does not promise that every application constraint or temporal fact is now represented correctly.

## Key takeaways

- Independent skill and language lists require all combinations in a combined table.
- 4NF controls non-trivial MVDs; 5NF controls join dependencies not implied by candidate keys.

## Further reading

- [Silberschatz, Korth and Sudarshan: relational database design](https://www.db-book.com/slides-dir/PDF-dir/ch7.pdf)
- [Fagin: multivalued dependencies and fourth normal form](https://research.ibm.com/publications/multivalued-dependencies-and-a-new-normal-form-for-relational-databases)
- [Fagin: Normal forms and relational database operators (1979)](https://research.ibm.com/publications/normal-forms-and-relational-database-operators)
- [Fagin: Domains and keys, section 5 definitions](https://s3.us.cloud-object-storage.appdomain.cloud/res-files/500-tods81.pdf)

questions.prompt: An employee has two skills and two languages. The business says the skill list and language list are independent. What must a flat employee/skill/language relation store for that employee?

options.text: Two rows pairing one skill with one language each
options.explanation: That records two specific pairs, so it cannot represent the required independent combinations.

options.text: Four rows, one for every skill and language combination
options.explanation: Correct. Independent lists require all four combinations. Splitting into employee/skill and employee/language relations removes that repetition and rejoins losslessly.

options.text: One row with arbitrary skill and language values
options.explanation: That loses the other values rather than modelling independent lists.

options.text: Four rows prove every possible employee relation is in 5NF
options.explanation: A sample does not establish the schema’s join dependencies, and four combinations do not by themselves prove 5NF.

questions.workedExample: For one employee, pair each of two skills with each of two languages: four combinations. Projecting the four rows onto employee/skill leaves two rows; projecting onto employee/language leaves two rows. Joining those projections on employee gives exactly the four original rows. The lossless split relies on the business rule that the lists are independent, rather than merely on today’s sample. A fifth-normal-form claim would additionally require examining all relevant join dependencies.
